extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature (researchers and scientifically literate audience across physics, physiology, archaeology, chemistry, and related fields)
extracted.subtask_description: Short scientific correspondence and brief reports that describe experimental methods, observations, and interpretive conclusions for publication in a general science journal (Nature). Emphasis on concise method description, key assumptions, and evidence supporting claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cambridge affiliation / admission regulation (language requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Graduates of other universities are excluded from privileges of affiliation (which include exemption from the Previous Examination and permission to take their degree on Part II of the Tripos after two years) if they have not taken Latin or Greek.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Cambridge would modify its regulations so that graduates who passed higher-standard entrance examinations at other universities (without Latin/Greek) could take the Cambridge B.A. on Part II after six terms, more advanced mathematical students from other universities would be able to use Cambridge instruction and examinations as a path into research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods to study ion binding in blood (overview of prior methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators have principally used compensatory dialysis of the serum (Rona, Michaelis, and co-workers) or filtration with pressure (Starling, Cushny, Richter-Quittner) to investigate whether salts in blood are ionised to the same extent as in aqueous solution and whether ions are absorbed by protein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These established methods are the principal comparisons for newer techniques (see EMF-based electrode methods). Each method has different assumptions and experimental constraints; authors compare results across methods to reach conclusions about ion binding.

rubrics_metrics.name: EMF-based determination of ionisation state of blood salts (sodium and chloride)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use electromotive-force measurements of electrodes (sodium amalgam electrode for Na, Ag/AgCl electrode for Cl) calibrated against known concentrations to infer concentrations of ions in serum and plasma under the assumption that salt ionisation equals that in aqueous solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: (1) prepare an electrode of known stable potential (e.g. a 0.2% sodium amalgam slowly decomposed as sodium electrode), (2) measure its E.M.F. against known NaCl solutions to obtain normal potential, (3) measure E.M.F. of serum/plasma samples, (4) recalculate total Na (or Cl) on assumption of same degree of ionisation as aqueous solution and compare to chemical analysis. Close agreement supports the conclusion that Na and Cl are 'as free as in an aqueous solution' (examples: calculated vs measured Na: 3.51/3.67 g vs 3.46/3.65 g per litre; Cl totals similarly close).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and calibration of sodium electrode (practical requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a slowly decomposed 0-2 per cent. sodium amalgam as a sodium electrode and establish its normal potential by measuring E.M.F. against sodium chloride solutions of known concentration and degree of ionisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the amalgam electrode is stable and calibrated before measuring biological samples; the calibration against known solutions is essential to translate E.M.F. readings into concentrations for biological fluids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimensional analysis: include shape/magnitude when attributing dimensions to area/volume
rubrics_metrics.description: When attributing dimensions to area (or volume), omit no magnitude necessary for capturing directionality; specifically, if you omit the important magnitude 'shape' in stating the dimensions of area, additional laws involving direction cannot be introduced into dimensional arguments and ambiguity results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain A (area) as an explicit magnitude (not replace by A/ℓ or similar) so that quantities measuring direction (shape, orientation) can be introduced; this resolves the ambiguity that otherwise makes some dimensional deductions (e.g. Child's high vacuum current law) impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling assumptions for resonance theory of hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: When modeling resonant behaviour of cochlear resonators and their contribution to auditory nerve stimuli, explicitly state assumptions: (a) sound-wave energy entering the ear in unit time is constant; (b) pitch is constant; (c) mean amplitude of all resonators in vibration at any one time is inversely proportional to the number in vibration; (d) the energy available for distribution is proportional to the time during which sound waves have been arriving (i.e. neglecting losses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also consider physiological factors of the auditory mechanism (threshold, latent period, simultaneous and successive contrast) and recognize that amplitude as well as number of resonators influences nerve response. Use these assumptions to estimate transient behaviour (e.g., in-tune resonators may reach ~90% of final amplitude in ~8 vibrations; rise to steady perceived intensity expected in ~10–20 vibrations). Provide illustrative tables and note lack of exactness where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small-scale towing-tank experimental design (Benjamin Franklin model)
rubrics_metrics.description: A trough experiment to study effect of water depth on boat speed: provision of a trough filled with water, a movable bottom board to vary depth while keeping surface level constant, a model boat of specified dimensions, a pulley-and-weight drive to pull the boat, and time-measurement by repetitive counting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design details given as an example: trough ~14 ft long, 6 in wide and deep; loose board adjustable by wedges to vary depth; boat ~6 in × 2.25 in × 1.25 in drawing 1 in water; motion driven by a fine thread over a small brass pulley with a known weight; time measured by repeated counts of tens and taking the median of repeated trials to correct counting errors. Repeat experiments at each depth and use the median (or average) to obtain more reliable results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental testing of Curie law under hysteresis-free conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: To test Curie's law (susceptibility k inversely proportional to absolute temperature T, so k·T = constant) in ferromagnetics near and below the critical temperature, experiments must be done under hysteresis-free conditions and allow for or eliminate effects of mutual molecular magnetic interactions and approach-to-saturation effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce observational data appropriately to see whether k·T is approximately constant in the ferromagnetic state (with a different constant magnitude than in paramagnetic state). Compare the ratio of constants in the two states to the kinetic energy per unit temperature associated with effective rotational degrees of freedom; corroborate with specific-heat measurements where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting molecular anisotropy in liquids via scattering theory and measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat polarised part of molecularly scattered light as a mass-effect from thermal fluctuations of density (Einstein–Smoluchowski formula) and the unpolarised part as a molecular effect proportional to molecular number density; predict that the ratio of unpolarised to polarised scattered light (Iu/(Ip + Iu)) is enhanced in liquids relative to vapours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the polarisation components of transverse scattering using a double-image prism and a Nicol prism; compare observed ratios (vapour vs liquid) to theoretical calculations and to measurements (example table: ethyl ether, benzene, chloroform). Use temperature dependence predictions (polarisation improves as critical temperature is approached) to design tests (e.g., experiments with benzene vapour and liquid as temperature varies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Archaeological standard: stratigraphical study to determine chronology and origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Stratigraphical study is essential to determine whether artefact types or domestic animals date from the beginning of lake settlements or were introduced later; typological hypotheses must be checked against stratigraphy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only detailed stratigraphical observation (recording layers and contexts) can settle questions such as introduction of spindle whorls, drilling techniques, appearance of particular pottery styles or animal domestication. Do not rely solely on typology without stratigraphical confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archaeological standard: detailed topographical survey and recording of submerged features
rubrics_metrics.description: When lake levels expose pile sites, undertake detailed topographical surveys recording positions of uncovered piles and those in shallow water to reconstruct site layout and town planning (e.g., island groupings, bridges, canals, breakwaters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record positions systematically (as at Greng and Geneva) to infer presence of stockades, breakwaters, and size/arrangement of settlements. Surveys should be planned to capture both exposed and submerged elements as lake levels change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archaeological field method: use of diving bell and preservation of finds
rubrics_metrics.description: For investigations on sites always submerged, use diving bells for in-situ observation and recovery; preserve all bones and artefacts found so that stratigraphical context is maintained and analyses (e.g., of domestication and dietary preferences) can be carried out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve and separately document bones and artefacts from each stratum. Detailed osteological analysis of preserved material (e.g., >4000 mammalian bones at St. Aubin) allows conclusions about domestication, species abundance, but must be interpreted in light of site-specific sampling and preservation biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vitamin assay: general quantitative requirements and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative estimation of vitamins presently requires many observations because individual variation in experimental animals is high; methods are tedious and not very accurate (antiscorbutic potency often only determined within ~25–50% accuracy). Low-potency materials require large doses that may interfere with other dietary requirements (e.g., protein), limiting accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the limitations: use many replicates; be aware that when potency is low the required test dose may disturb other aspects of the diet and confound results; interpret modest differences cautiously given large measurement variance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vitamin A assay (Zilva & Miura method) — procedural standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Method to estimate Vitamin A potency: keep young rats on a diet totally deficient in Vitamin A until they have ceased to grow, then ascertain the minimum dose of the test material that will induce definite and steady growth for four weeks; reject animals which do not cease to grow within three weeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administer the test material quantitatively (not merely mixed into the ration) to achieve greater uniformity in results. Use uniform selection criteria (reject animals that fail to show expected prescreen responses) to reduce variability. This method yields more consistent comparative potencies (example: cod-liver oil found ~200–250 times as potent as butter).
